maintopic: OVERAGES SHOWN BY COUNTRY ELEVATORS DURING PERIOD OF FIVE-YEAR POOL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: OVERAGES SHOWN BY COUNTRY ELEVATORS DURING PERIOD OF FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Has the minister examined the situation in respect of overages shown by country elevator companies in their operations over the past five years? If so, does he consider that any action is necessary in this connection?
Eight Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of this question. I have certainly looked into the matter of these overages. In the case of wheat, I find that out of 1,427,587,096 bushels of producers' wheat handled in the five-year pool, there were overages of 3,470,789 bushels, or -24 of one per cent in country elevators, and 2,151,149 bushels, or -15 of one per cent in terminals. Upon further examination I find that the bulk of these overages occurred in the crop years 1945-46 and 1946-47, which followed about three years of congested conditions in the elevators in which no weigh-over had been possible in many of the elevators. This situation was common to both the producer-owned and the privately-owned companies. Because the companies had not been able to weigh over their own houses that were congested, the overages in question actually occurred over some seven or eight years of operation rather than in the five-year pool period only.
Those who are familiar with the provisions of the Canada Grain Act know that the board of grain commissioners have no power to weigh-over country elevators or to take possession of overages that occur. I believe it would be mistaken policy to take such powers, because the principle of seizing overages implies that the crown should make good on losses. Because of the competition prevailing among the country elevator companies, the underwriting of losses would lead to competitive abuses in that direction.
Where the board of grain commissioners do have power to act is in the setting of the shrinkage allowances in determining the net weight of wheat delivered at the elevators. It is common knowledge that there is invisible loss in the handling of grain. To compensate for this, a shrinkage allowance is made on


all grain taken into the elevator. A shrinkage table is displayed in a prominent position in each elevator. From November, 1923, until the end of the 1947-48 crop year, a shrinkage allowance of one-half of one per cent on receipts of straight grade wheat at country elevators was in effect.
As soon as the board of grain commissioners were able to review the country elevator operations and found that substantial overages had occurred during the period of congestion, they lowered the shrinkage allowance on straight grade wheat from one-half of one per cent to one-quarter of one per cent, effective for the crop years 1948-49 and
1949- 50.	Operating under these reduced shrinkage schedules, country elevators showed a wheat shortage of -02 per cent on total handlings for 1948-49, and a very slight overage of -002 per cent for the 1949-50 crop season.
In these circumstances, the board felt justified in partly meeting the representation of elevator companies for increased allowance, and accordingly adjusted the shrinkage rate on wheat from one-quarter of one per cent to three-eighths of one per cent for the
1950-	51 crop year. The effect of this recent revision in shrinkage schedules will not be known until the elevators furnish their sworn statements to the board on their 1950-51 operations.
The point I am making is this. The board of grain commissioners acted over three years ago to correct a situation which was revealed when the country elevator congestion was relieved. The action they took at that time effectively wiped out the overages in the subsequent years of operation. I have every confidence in the ability of the board of grain commissioners to maintain effective oversight of this situation. As a matter of fact, I have asked the board if any further action could or should be taken, and they have advised me that no further action at this time is necessary. The whole problem of overages is reviewed annually, and will be a matter of further study at the board's tariff meeting to be held in July, when they should have the results of this year's operations.

The fact that the Red Chinese government has now made some bilateral arrangement with Tibet, which borders on the northern provinces of India, and that the information concerning the possibility of a highway from the eastern boundaries of Russia to the Orient itself-
The Depuiy Chairman: Order. I believe the hon. member will realize that he cannot initiate a debate on that question on the resolution which is before the committee.

I want to say a word at this point concerning the somewhat abbreviated conversation I had yesterday with the minister. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I shall answer that now. Yesterday, in answer to my hon. friend's question, I said that one swallow does not make a summer. If he were as familiar as I am with the proposed expenditures on defence for the coming year he would not be unduly concerned about the apparent surplus for one month out of the twelve. This year there is a surplus of receipts over expenditures of something in the order of $120 million. But again I emphasize the point that we are a long way from the end of this fiscal year, and many of the expenditures for our defence program are just beginning to come in. So far as I am concerned, I have nothing to apologize for and nothing to defend in the present position of my budgetary estimates.

My only comment on what the minister has said is that, in so far as he gives last year as a warranty for what is done this year, the answer is not a good one, because he proved to be terribly wrong last year.
May I have an answer to my question with respect to emergency famine relief in India?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Possibly I might say a word in reply to the question of the hon. gentleman, although I confess my inability to deal with this matter in all its details in. the absence of a little bit more notice than I have been given. The situation with regard to famine in India and Canada's possible contribution to the relief of that situation is briefly as follows.
As the committee knows, some weeks ago, when this matter was brought to our attention as a government, we indicated to the representative of the government of India that we would be in a position to make available to the government and the people of India low-grade wheat, No. 5 and No. 6, which was the only wheat at that time in our possession. That wheat would have been given to India as part of our contribution under the Colombo plan.

The reason we made that offer in that way at that time has, I think, already been given to the house. The Indian government at that time indicated that they would prefer not to accept the offer, because they had some doubts as to the advisability of wheat of that type getting into their rationing system. They thought that it might create misunderstanding thereby, and indicated that they would prefer to wait until better class wheat would be available from the next harvest. However, subsequently, we got in touch again with the acting Indian high commissioner in Ottawa, and with the Indian government through our representative in New Delhi, to inquire whether the Indian government would be inclined to receive as a gift-quite apart from anything we might do under the Colombo plan-a contribution of the only wheat which was available to us. We thought that if it were given in that form, it might be used as famine relief exclusively. It could go into the famine areas, be given to those suffering from famine, would not be included in the ration and might not create the difficulties that the Indian government had previously mentioned.
Would it be included in the amount to be given under the Colombo plan?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. It would be in addition to anything we might do under the Colombo plan; it would be sent to India as a gift for famine relief and be distributed as famine relief only.
How many bushels?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We first inquired whether that procedure would meet with the wishes of the Indian government. I think it was only yesterday, or at least a day or so ago, that we received information from the government of India to the effect that while they greatly appreciated an offer of this kind, they would still prefer to wait until wheat of a better quality might be available. Possibly one reason for the stand they took at this time was an arrangement which they informed us they had been making with neighbouring countries, for the supply of additional quantities of rice which they hoped would tide them over the period of greatest danger. They had also been making arrangements for food supplies of other kinds from neighbouring countries. In the circumstances, therefore, they thought that possibly they would suspend any decision on our offer of a gift of No. 5 or No. 6 wheat. Meanwhile we have been canvassing the situation in Canada as to whether other kinds of food might be available for Indian famine relief, in particular special health foods.
Interim Supply
Canned milk or dried milk?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Dried milk is one of the types of food we have been looking into. That matter is still under active consideration. We have also made some inquiries as to whether it would be possible to divert to India from other customers better grades of wheat which could be replaced to those customers later on when the new crop becomes available in Canada. Those matters are still under consideration.
I therefore think I can say, Mr. Chairman, that we have not lost sight of this matter and that we are attempting to do what is possible to show in a practical way our good will to the people of India in the extremely difficult situation which faces them.

I should like to ask a supplementary question. Has consideration been given to the sending of medical supplies to India? In addition, I understand that there are a number of organizations in Canada which are anxious to take it upon themselves to send food and supplies of one kind or another as a gift to India. I think there is a misunderstanding in the country. I have heard people ask this question: Why will they not accept No. 5 and No. 6 wheat? I believe the real explanation is that such flour as can be extracted, such as it is, cannot be used in the type of flat cake bread baked over an open fire that is commonly used in the rural parts of India.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am not an authority on this matter. Maybe my friend the Minister of Agriculture knows more than I do about baking bread in India. In addition, I think the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre were unfair to him, because the hon. member for Temiscouata made it clear that private members should not be criticized for looking after the small post offices and those rendering public service to the people. That is what he said. He said he interfered only- he made that quite clear-when people complained, and he felt it was in accordance with his duty. He also made it clear that he replaced or recommended replacements in certain post offices only where the former Liberal appointee, for no reason whatever but politics, had been discharged by the succeeding government. These were the only cases in which he interfered at all. He also said that if there were no complaints in operation he never interfered at all, or even visited the postmasters, which I am sure some hon. members, even in the C.C.F. party, cannot say that they have not done.
He also made it clear that he had not recommended any persons merely because they were among his supporters, but only those perfectly qualified to occupy a position in the Post Office Department. I was greatly interested in the remarks that have been made this afternoon up until now. I was, however, somewhat surprised by the objection made to the text of the new act which states that the Postmaster General shall administer, superintend land manage the Canada Post Office. The reason for my astonishment is this. We are talking a great deal about democracy. We are sending our sons to fight for democracy. The way that we apply democracy in our form of government is to entrust the administration of the country to a group of men chosen from the ranks of those who have been elected by the people at the previous election and chosen by the Prime Minister who usually heads the group which has the majority in the house. My objection is not that they would administer too much. My experience over the past is that too many of them are too inclined to pass the administration to subordinate officers or deputy ministers or officials. This clause is found generally in the acts creating all the different departments. How it is applied is another thing to look into, and that deserves the remarks made by some of my hon. friends; but the text of it and the powers it gives I think are justly given to the minister. I think

it is the duty of a minister to know his department, to administer his department. After all, he is the one who is elected. He represents the majority of the people of Canada who have sent the government here, of which he is a member, to take charge of the administration.
I do not approve the tendency of many cabinet ministers in the past-now I am not criticising anybody in particular-of having the administration carried on the shoulders of deputy ministers who may be able men, but who are not responsible to the people of Canada directly. Therefore I do not think we should be scandalized at all by the powers given to the minister. That these powers be not used solely on the basis of party politics is quite right. I would be against the appointment of government officials of a department if we took into consideration only their political affiliation, but we have the civil service commission, and they watch that very closely.
The only point of controversy seems to be the appointment of postmasters in rural areas or in small post offices where the revenue is low and where many other considerations besides ability need to be taken into account. When you appoint a postal clerk in the city he goes to the post office and works there. When you appoint a postmaster in a village he must have the post office in his own home. Therefore there are many more considerations that have to be taken into account.
I think it would be hard for anybody to suggest a system that would do away entirely with the minister having to take some suggestions somewhere from people who know the constituency well. That the man should be recommended only by a member of parliament is not enough. On the other hand, how will you establish rules to appoint postmasters in rural constituencies? First of all, you must have a man who has a home in the centre of the village. The government does not supply the post office. No matter how able a man may be, no matter how clever he may be, if he lives two miles away from the centre he will be of no use to the village if he is appointed a postmaster. Therefore you have to select a man who lives in the centre of the village. Then, you may have some people who are of relative value intellectually, but they may have had trouble in the past in their own business or otherwise; it may be that a man is not reliable.
I do not think that politics should be the main factor or should enter into consideration as the main qualification, but I do not see any objection to members of parliament, as the
Post Office Act
hon. member for Red Deer said a moment ago, having something to say. They are the ones who know the constituency. They have been elected, good or bad as we may think of one another. We have been elected in the various parties in the house by the people of Canada, and the people of Canada cannot all be wrong. We respect one another here in the House of Commons, and I think we might also respect our suggestions to the Postmaster General for the appointment of a man in a rural district. That it should be the only basis, no. I agree with that. It is not right; but I cannot find a suitable system of appointing these men through the civil service commission. I have looked into the matter myself at times when I could not get the man I wanted appointed, but I could not find a proper system of appointment through the civil service commission.
I come now to the mail couriers. On February 20, 1947, I made a good speech on the subject, but I will not repeat it today. I only want to refer the minister and the house to it. Here is another case where it is very hard to apply any rule as to how the appointments should be made. Some people say that these men should be made permanent, but permanent on what basis? Today a man is appointed on the tender system. He has a contract. The time comes when the figure at which he has tendered is not sufficient. He has equipped himself. He has the winter rigs, the snowmobiles, or whatever you call them. He has all the necessary equipment. To get a raise of $100 or $200, he has to resign. Then, new tenders are called. A new man who just wants to get the contract and does not realize the work entailed, a man who is less responsible in many ways, will submit a lower tender. He may think he can use for that purpose one of his horses and a junior son to handle the mail at ridiculously low prices. I do not think it is fair. On the other hand, what is the basis on which to choose rural mail couriers outside of politics entirely? You cannot have a competition. Would you choose the man who has the best looking horse or the best looking car to do the job? How can you judge the qualifications of a man to carry the mail in a rural district? We now do it by tenders which is a suitable way when the contract is vacant by expiration or if a man wants to resign his job. If he resigns his job, very well. But when there is a need for reclassification will you force the man, as under the present law, to let tenders be called and take the risk of having gone to all this expense to equip himself well, and lose the contract to an irresponsible person?

Post Office Act
In this regard I think we have to follow the example of what happened when the department resorted to the sort of system which is envisaged here, namely, that of the Postmaster General adjusting prices up to a certain amount? During the war that was done under the War Measures Act. I think most hon. members will agree that there were no abuses when the prioes were reclassified, and I may say that we had a difficult time to get them raised. I think a given price in the district was more or less understood as being fair, and an amount much below that price was raised to the average price by the department officials. I have done that in a number of cases without ever going to the Postmaster General. I am not talking against any of those who had the job before, but I did not care to go there because I thought I would rather go to the official who knew that particular branch quite well and appeal to his good sense and show the iproblem to him. In this regard I may say that in my province, and I think throughout Canada, the people have confidence in the present Postmaster General. He is a man of intelligence and integrity. He is a hard-working man.
I would not say he is the first Postmaster General who knows about his department, but he works very hard to get to know and understand the whole working of his department, and I think it is for the good of the country that a member of the government should go so deeply into his own department as to know what it is all about and what is going on. He should be congratulated on that. I do not think anybody here need worry about the provision under which the minister can do these things, because we had an example, as I say, of what happened under the War Measures Act. The cost of living was increasing. There was difficulty in getting material, and the men were asked to carry the mail over winter roads, over hills and far distances at very low prices. There was no way for them to get a reclassification in their prices under the Post Office Act. Reclassifications were made, if I remember correctly, in a number of cases under the War Measures Act. I have yet to hear of any injustices being done or that prices were very high. We had to fight every time to get very meagre increases from the department's officials. And I think it is right; they have to make sure no abuses are committed.
I admit however that it is not fitting to place in the act anything detrimental to the good of the country, or to leave in it any implication that there is danger of patronage

ruining the department. I do suggest however that the elected representatives of the people are the ones who would know something about their constituencies, and who would be best able to advise the minister and to express their opinions respecting matters affecting their constituencies. That is particularly true of hon. members who have returned to the house on many occasions. I suggest that they are well informed in matters affecting their constituencies and are often better informed than officials stationed at Ottawa who must pass judgment on cases concerning which they have received a meagre report from an inspector who may have spent no more than half an hour in the locality in question. On the other hand the member may have lived there all his life, or at any rate he would know it well.
I say in conclusion therefore that I have no fear for the fate of the country, even if the bill is passed as it now stands.

It is my understanding that the present measure scraps completely the old act. If in this bill some portions of the old act are embodied, they appear here only after a thorough process of face-lifting and varnishing so that, as I see it, they will give far greater control and power to the Postmaster General and his officials, or directly to the government itself. The regulations will come up from time to time as discussion of the bill proceeds.
One subject that has been discussed for years, and mentioned again yesterday by some hon. members, was that of the injustices done to rural mail couriers. After reading the bill I am convinced that the injustices they have suffered will now be worse than ever, because we will find when we discuss the regulations that control is now entirely vested in the Postmaster General.

When I first discussed the matter in 1945 or 1946 the then postmaster general promised a committee to look into the matter of rural mail couriers. That committee never was set up, and these matters have had to be discussed privately. The problem grows worse and, because of the measure of inflation we now have, the condition with respect to tenders and contracts

is not improving. When an effort is made to get low tenders someone is going to be scalded in the operation.
I believe I can speak with most authority about my own constituency, because I know the conditions there so far as the rural mail couriers are concerned. In the dual constituency of Queens we have seventy-nine rural mail couriers, and in addition we have five districts in which there are twenty-six couriers, making a total of one hundred and five.
I should like first to deal with contracts in my constituency that have been let for distances ranging from six miles up to fifty, and in this connection I should like to place on record some of the dealings concerning the men employed. I would draw attention first to what might be called inconsistencies, or perhaps discrimination, that exist in connection with the tenders and contracts awarded. These men are all responsible and trustworthy, and I should like to mention a few of them in particular.
I want to mention one in particular in the constituency of Queens, and I should like the Postmaster General to consider whether or not it is fair treatment. I do not wish to mention names so I will call it exhibit No. 1. Mr. A, a courier, drives eighteen miles, serves fifty-nine boxes and receives an annual fee of $1,560. Mr. B, no distance from this other man, drives 17-5 miles, serves forty-two boxes and receives $591.27. For driving half a mile farther A gets a lot more money. It is true he serves seventeen more boxes but for driving half a mile more and serving seventeen more boxes he gets $969 more than Mr. B. I should like the Postmaster General to say whether that is fair treatment. Another point I should like to make is that the man who is receiving the highest payment is not getting one nickel too much for the service he is rendering.
He receives $1,560 for making six trips a week or approximately 310 trips in a year for which he receives the princely sum of $5 a day. If he uses a car, we all know what the expenses of operation would be and the depreciation; but if he uses a horse and carriage in the summertime and a horse and sleigh in the winter there is also a cost there. A horse cannot be fed at the present time for less than $1 a day, and in addition there are other costs. The man would only be receiving at the highest $3 a day for wages for himself. Contrast that with the wages of the employees in the department, and you will find that this man even at the highest price is only getting a bare living wage.
What about the other poor fellow with his contract for 17-5 miles? For doing almost

the same work they only pay him $590 or $1.90 per day for himself and his horse. He would not be able to buy a half ton truck because at the end of four years he would not have the truck paid for even if the whole amount he received was paid on it. There must be some way to overcome this situation. Such great discrimination should not exist.

But I do want to refer to the postal rate on newspapers. This was dealt with yesterday by some speakers, but I do not believe the position of newspapers in my province of Prince Edward Island can be compared with the position of newspapers in the larger centres. There is one newspaper in Prince Edward Island with a circulation of 13,000 or more which is a fairly large circulation in a province with the population of Prince Edward Island. It will have to find some other way of getting their papers to the public.
As a solution I suggest to the Postmaster General that he institute a zoning system for the carriage of newspapers similar to that in effect for parcel post. Such a system would give this newspaper a chance to live. When you consider that a newspaper that distributes 8,000 copies through one post office must pay that office $50 a day, sufficient to pay three or four employees, it means something. First I should like to deal with the matter of the rural mail couriers. The position of these couriers is the result of the tender system. All the cases that have been cited are under tender. The different routes have different characteristics that must be considered, not only by the department but by the person making the tender. The length of the route is one factor, the number of boxes is another; then the type and variety of equipment necessary to operate the route 80709-22?
Post Office Act
must be considered, as well as the condition of the roads and the volume of the mail; consideration must be given to the time of day when the service is required, to the climatic conditions, to the availability and use of equipment, to the necessity of combining the route with other types of transportation, and to general economic conditions. All these questions have to be taken into consideration by the person making the tender for a particular route. The route immediately next to it might be completely different, but in each case it is the person offering the tender to the department that must make the appraisal of the conditions of that particular route. The department receives tenders from various persons, and chooses the lowest of those tenders. The department cannot be accused of imposing a rate on one particular courier, because he is the one who has made the offer. If his offer is too low he has the sole responsibility for that condition.
A long time ago the department realized that the tender system was not the best system that could be devised. We have been looking at various ways of curing the situation. We thought of a zoning system, but that would be still worse than the situation as it exists today. If we were to level off all the contracts in one given area, that would mean that those which were above the average before the levelling off would receive less than they were entitled to receive, whereas those below the average would get more than they were entitled to get. There would be a discrepancy, and there would be injustice. That was one of the reasons for suggesting section 23 in the postal act. We hope that it will produce the necessary results.
The hon. member for Queens said that in 1945 my predecessor suggested a committee be formed, and after that nothing happened. I remind the hon. member that in 1946 the Supplemental Payments Act was introduced, and bonuses were given to all the couriers who applied for them. In the end, about eighty per cent of the couriers did.

On March 31, 1949, when the law was finally repealed, eighty per cent of all contracts had been re-adjusted.
Dealing with rates on newspapers, the hon. member suggested a zoning system. We have examined the question of zoning newspapers. If a system similar to the parcel post zoning system were adopted, the rates now suggested for newspapers would be applied to the first zone. Any additional zone would involve an extra charge, because we have to meet

Post Office Act
the deficit that we have. The purpose of the proposed rate is to reduce the deficit in handling newspapers and periodicals. Unless the additional zones in the zoning system produced the additional revenue the purpose of the new rates would be lost. The extra charges would fall chiefly on the national magazines, as those are the publications which have dominion-wide distribution. They are possibly less able to bear the additional charges than are the large dailies, distribution of which is chiefly restricted to the province of publication or the adjacent province.
Zoning would involve increased costs to the department, as it would be necessary to segregate newspapers according to zones so as to check the weights and charges involved. It would also mean extra cost to the publisher, as he would have to segregate the newspapers according to zones and calculate the postage at the different postal rates in effect. In the United States, where zoning has been adopted, the deficit for second-class material is over $160 million per year. While it is not intended for one moment to attribute this loss to zoning, there is no doubt that some of it is caused by extra administration and handling costs which the zoning arrangement entails.
There is a final argument against zoning. In my opinion the zoning of newspapers in this country would create a balkanization of Canada. At the present time the Post Office Department is helping to a great extent in the dissemination of news. There is nothing in the rates that would prevent a paper from British Columbia going to the province of Quebec or a paper from Halifax going to Toronto. The rates are the same. It is in that way that the thoughts of the people out west will be known by those in the east, and vice versa. If we were going to make small states of each province, or if we were going to make small areas of about two hundred miles, I am sure that the newspapers of the area would remain in that area. I am absolutely opposed to that because it would be against the unity of Canada.

I should like to be on record as opposing the new increase in rates for daily and weekly newspapers. I am opposing the increase as a Quebec member, because I think this new amendment will affect my province more than any other in Canada. As we all know, in the province of Quebec the daily papers are confined to the four largest cities: Montreal, Quebec, Three Rivers and Sherbrooke. As a result, most of their distribution-at least outside Montreal-is done through the mails, and all the literature and news that the rural people of my province read must go through the postal service. I realize that some people may say that our dailies are good business concerns; but it must also be remembered that they are really rendering great services in giving us the news and some good editorials.
I think the rural people deserve better treatment than they are getting, because we can be sure that in the end these increases will be borne by the ordinary people. In many places the newspaper is about the only literature and the only news service that the people can afford. I want to protest against this increase, in particular with regard to the small dailies. I know that in Montreal we have a few dailies which are good newspapers but which have small circulations. The main circulation of some of them is outside the city of Montreal, and they depend to the extent of more than 50 per cent on their rural customers. These newspapers are rendering a real service to the country and to their communities. I would not be surprised if the new increase in the rates would put them out of business completely. Mr. Chairman, I have
had considerable criticism to oiler with regard to the Post Office Department; but at this time I am happy to be able to congratulate the minister on one important step. I was happy to hear him make the statement last night that the letter carriers who have been working for longer than eight hours a day may rest assured that they will be paid for the extra hours worked. I was also very happy to learn that steps are being taken to rectify a situation which exists in the Toronto area regarding mail delivery service. I am quite sure that nothing that the department has done since the institution of the one delivery a day system will do more to raise the morale of the employees than will the assurance which the minister gave the house last night regarding the accumulated overtime which these men whose walks have not yet been checked are building up for themselves and will receive when their walks are adjusted.
I want to assure the minister that the situation as far as the Toronto postal service is concerned is still bad. It has deteriorated within the past two months. I myself have had occasions when letters posted in our post office in the building, letters that I posted on Tuesday, were not delivered in Toronto until Saturday morning. I have had a number of instances of that kind. I have today one example that I presume is an accident of some kind. I received a letter today that I mailed here in the post office on February 3. It went through the Ottawa post office on February 3. The first Toronto date stamp on it is May 17, three and a half months after. The addressee had moved in the meantime. The letter that was stamped in Toronto on May 17 returned to me this morning with the Ottawa stamp, May 30. That I take it is one of those accidents which should not occur in the post office but which probably do, and would under any system. I take it that is an exception, but the length of time which is required
(Mr. Balcer.]
for the ordinary daily mail to be delivered in Toronto is rather exasperating.
Businessmen tell me that if they want a letter from Ottawa delivered in Toronto the following day, which has been the usual practice for years, they must now use the special delivery stamp to assure that the letter is delivered within twenty-four or thirty-six hours after it is mailed in Ottawa. Therefore there is a real need for a thorough check-up on the service in the Toronto district. I am quite confident that the restoration of the morale of the post office employees will do more to improve that service than anything else will.
Reference has already been made to the wages which letter carriers are receiving. I think the minister will probably have to face up to the question that in the competition which the post office is meeting today in regard to employment more and more difficulty will be experienced in getting reliable letter carriers or to retain in the service many of his best and most experienced men at their present wages. The minister will agree that in the Toronto district there have been, within the past two or three months, a considerable number of resignations by letter carriers who up to a few months ago regarded themselves as being permanently employed in the Post Office Department, and were satisfied with their working conditions, but who have since resigned because of the upheaval which has taken place within their work. I feel as sure as an earlier speaker who threw out certain suggestions that the minister may have to give consideration to a revision of the wages which are being offered today in the advertisements for letter carriers, and that revisions will be needed to restore the efficiency of the department.
While I am very happy to hear that these men will receive overtime pay, I want to remind the minister that if this were a private enterprise company or an industrial employer they would think in terms of overtime pay not at regular rates but at time and a half, and in some instances double time. There are very few industries in the country today, very few industries are left, in which employees are required to work three or four hours a day overtime without getting more than regular overtime pay for those overtime hours.

In previous debates on the Post Office Department I called attention to the fact that neither in Forest Hill village nor in York township have we as yet a single postal station. Here is a community of over 100,000 people. Their postal stations are situated in the municipality of the city of Toronto. There is a real need for one or two postal stations north of the present postal station on St. Clair avenue west and west of the present postal station on north Yonge street. Because Toronto happens to envelop the village of Forest Hill and York township the people in those two municipalities must travel to city post offices to transact any post office business that cannot be carried on in the small sub-post offices located in stores throughout the riding. I know surveys have been made and various reasons have been given.
During the war years no new post offices could be constructed, but I have heard of some being built since the war. I sincerely hope there is no relation whatever between the fact that neither Forest Hill nor York township has a postal station and the other fact that that particular riding has not at any time in its history elected a Liberal to the House of Commons. I am sure that even if a Progressive Conservative member makes a request to the government, it is patronage that must be condemned: the only thing that is right, the only thing that is honest, the only thing that can be done in the public interest, according to the hon. member and some others in his group, is what is being asked for by the C.C.F,
Let us look at what happens in Saskatchewan-how the Conservatives, the Liberals and the Social Crediters are martyrized by the government of Saskatchewan.
